#4802. Can You Lose 10 Pounds In A Month? Experts Share 15 Tips For Safe Weight Loss In 30 Days

It only makes sense to want to give your weight loss journey everything you’ve got. And, if you’re into big goals, you may wonder if it’s safe to lose 10 pounds in a month.

Here's the truth: The average person cannot safely lose 10 pounds in a month, says Michael Glickman, MD, a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness. Losing weight at this aggressive of a pace can raise your risk of developing gallstones (painful deposits of digestive fluid in the gallbladder) and up the odds that you’ll regain the weight down the line, he says. (Neither of those are ideal!)

Meet the experts: Michael Glickman, MD, is a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness. Michael Hamlin, CSCS, is a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness.

Of course, everyone is different and a lot depends on your starting weight. Also, you can still have aggressive goals when it comes to weight loss—it’s just that 10 pounds in a too-short timeframe is a tricky benchmark for most people. So, how much weight can you safely lose in a month—and how should you even go about it? Here’s what experts suggest.

The timeline will be different for everyone, given factors like starting weight, genetics, nutrition, activity level, stress, and more. But Dr. Glickman says to give yourself anywhere from two to three months to hit that 10-pounds-lost goal. “For some, this could take longer, so be compassionate with your body and prioritize what’s best for your health,” he says.

When it comes to how much weight is safe to lose at a given time, stick to one to two pounds per week, says Dr. Glickman. “Some people can shed weight more quickly in the first month after instituting a lower calorie and healthy diet, however much of the weight loss on the scale will have been due to water weight.”

If you have obesity and are revamping your eating habits, along with starting an exercise program after being fairly sedentary, you may see bigger gains early on than someone with a lower starting weight who isn’t making drastic changes.

First things first: A safe way to lose weight is a holistic and multi-factorial approach that involves optimal nutrition, frequent exercise, stress reduction, and adequate sleep, says Dr. Glickman. It's not necessarily about eating less but being conscious of the diversity of plants in your diet, and the avoidance of processed foods, refined oils, and refined carbohydrates, he explains.

On top of that, apply sustainable healthy changes to your routine that you enjoy, says Michael Hamlin, CSCS, a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness. Maybe that means attending a workout class with friends twice a week, cooking a plant-based dinner with your partner, or throwing on your favorite podcast and going for a solo walk.

Sleep deprivation promotes an increase in ghrelin, your hunger hormone, which can trigger late night snacking, ultimately increasing your daily caloric intake, says Dr. Glickman. So do your best to get seven to nine hours of sleep per night. Not only that, getting more sleep helps you feel more energized, so you can add more activity to your day.

It may sound simple, but 30 minutes of daily walking can do wonders, says Dr. Glickman. “It isn’t about calorie burning—it’s about the mobility, the happy hormones your brain releases, and the physiological anti-inflammatory responses that have long-term impacts on your weight.”

Getting daily steps in has health benefits ranging from lowering your risk of developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease to helping you live longer. While any movement is good, moving at a brisk pace is the best way to get in all those extra perks.

Plant diversity has been shown to have the most beneficial impact on the gut microbiome, which influences your metabolic set point (the body’s preferred weight), insulin levels, and fat storage, says Dr. Glickman. Plant-based diets are also linked to a lower risk of developing heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, making this a big win for your overall health, too.

His suggestion? Try a plant-based day or meal per week to ensure you’re supporting your gut microbiome and loading up on the veggies.

It’s best to consult a doctor or registered dietitian to determine your daily caloric needs since it depends on your age, gender, activity level, muscle mass, current weight, and the amount of calories you burn at rest (a.k.a. your basal metabolic rate), says Hamlin. From there, they can determine a slight calorie deficit, or how many calories you need in a day to lose one to two pounds a week, he explains.

While you’re waiting for a consult, check out the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases’ online body weight planner. It asks you to enter some basic information like your current weight, your ideal weight, and your activity level, and provides what your daily calorie goals should be to help you get there.

“Stress can lead to increased hunger hormones and an elevated metabolic set point,” says Dr. Glickman. Higher levels of the stress hormone cortisol can create stubborn fat distribution around the abdomen, he adds.

Although this one is often easier said than done, to help combat stress and anxiety, try relaxation techniques like meditation, yoga, and journaling. And, of course, if you’re struggling with stress management, consider reaching out to a mental health therapist for individual guidance on navigating everything.

“Sometimes we can mistake the feeling of thirst for hunger, so make sure to stay hydrated throughout the day, especially during and after exercise,” Dr. Glickman says. Women should drink about 11.5 cups (2.7 liters) of fluids a day, per Mayo Clinic. (Note: That total can come from food and liquids.)

Strength training has a significant impact on your metabolism and fat burning capabilities, studies show, so incorporate resistance training at least three days a week, says Dr. Glickman. Just take note that because strength training builds muscle, you may notice little or even no overall weight change at times, even though you are losing fat. (Not sure where to start with your strength training journey? Try Women's Health's The Woman's Guide To Strength Training: Dumbbells.)

HIIT workouts burn a ton of calories and can change your body composition while building muscle, says Hamlin. In fact, women who incorporated HIIT programming achieved similar body composition and aerobic capacity results in half the time as women who did moderate-intensity workouts, a 2017 study published in the Journal of Diabetes Research found.

Fiber helps regulate blood sugar levels, prevent insulin resistance and diabetes, and is an excellent source of nutrition for healthy bacteria in the gut, says Dr. Glickman. High-fiber foods like vegetables are also filling without overloading on the calories, explains Hamlin. You can get fiber in powder or supplement form, but your best (and healthiest) bet is from plants, adds Dr. Glickman.

Weight gain is linked with the consumption of highly processed and packaged foods, Dr. Glickman says. “This includes any food item in a wrapper with ingredients you can’t pronounce, even if the calories and carbohydrates seem appealing,” he explains. “Always choose whole foods over packaged ones.”

Do your best to prioritize cooking at home to eliminate sneaky fats, sugars, and processed ingredients that are not listed on a menu, says Dr. Glickman.

Focus on the quality of food on your plate and aim for three hearty meals a day that include a small amount of complex carbohydrates (root veggies and whole grains), a moderate amount of high-quality protein (fish, chicken, eggs, and tofu), and lots of plant-based fiber, says Dr. Glickman.

Alcoholic drinks lack nutritional value and are usually packed with calories, so it’s best to scale back on booze, says Hamlin. When you drink alcohol, it also immediately goes to the liver where it’s prioritized as an energy source, so your body burns alcohol cals first. Not only that, alcohol also lowers your inhibitions and raises the odds you’ll eat more than you need to feel satiated.

To help with accountability, Hamlin suggests using a food journal or app to track your meals. This will give you a better understanding and awareness of how many calories you’re consuming and at which meal. Research shows this is an effective way to lose weight, too. One study found that people who tracked their meals at least five days of each week had “significant and sustained weight loss” over time compared to people who tracked less or inconsistently.

It can take time for your stomach to recognize when it’s full, so pause in between portions before deciding if you actually want more, says Hamlin. You can either pre-pack your meals with smaller portion sizes or use smaller plates to provide a visual cue. One scientific analysis of 14 studies found that people who ate smaller portions had a “substantial” drop in how many calories they ate each day.

Think long-term about weight loss and establish a goal that is realistic for your lifestyle, says Hamlin. Your goals might take time and patience, but that’s okay, he adds. “Weight loss isn't solely about a caloric deficit, because the body is a super complex piece of machinery, and we can't simply boil all of weight loss down to calories in versus calories out.”

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#4799. How market depth shapes the price of a weekend Bitcoin sale

Over 14 hours, Bitcoin traded on Kraken’s Canadian dollar market at an average 37.3% discount to a benchmark based on the exchange’s US dollar trades.

A narrow bid-ask spread can conceal the cost of selling 10 Bitcoin. If the best bid covers only part of the order, a desk seeking to sell the full amount immediately must accept lower prices for the balance.

From Friday evening to Saturday morning, 592.24 Bitcoin (BTC) changed hands on Kraken’s Canadian dollar market at an average of 51,886 Canadian dollars per coin. At the Bank of Canada’s Friday exchange rate, the benchmark was CA$82,798 per coin.

The price available to sellers varied even within a single second on Saturday. On the Canadian dollar market, the first of 104 fills fetched CA$31,000 per coin. Across the 10.42 BTC sold, the average was CA$25,505, nearly 18% lower.

#4798. 76 AD-Approved Interior Photographers in the Northeast

Grand staircases. Cozy breakfast nooks. Color-drenched walls. You name it, these interior photographers in the Northeast have shot it, in daylight and darkness, maximizing views of the park or the coast, the backyard or the city street far below. Their images are portraits of homes, capturing a space’s personality and highlighting the talents of its designer. Read on to meet AD-approved interior photographers in the Northeast (and, in many cases, beyond).

A beachfront home in Santa Barbara, California.

Classical proportions and carefully composed details give William Abranowicz’s interior photos the poise of a still life. His background as a fine art printer shows in images that reward looking beyond the statement furniture to the smaller objects around it.

This vibrant San Francisco home designed by Noz Nozawa is sometimes called “the Rainbow House.”

Brittany Ambridge makes colorful rooms shine and white rooms look luminous without losing the details that give them dimension. Her lighting approach draws on techniques learned shooting film, translating a home’s atmosphere whether the mood is airy and expansive, or bold and colorful. She has worked with talents including Jeremiah Brent, Nate Berkus, Charlotte Moss, and Gachot Studios.

Find your next creative collaborator using the AD PRO Sourcebook. Start exploring top interior photographers, stylists, decorative painters, millworkers, and more now.

The living room of Kate Upton and Justin Verlander’s penthouse in New York

Dramatic natural lighting is often heightened and accentuated in Gieves Anderson’s photographs, in both moody, highly patterned rooms as well as light and airy spaces. He knows just how to make the most of a perfectly cast shadow.

An interior at the Maison Brummell Majorelle in Marrakech, Morocco.

Trained in classical and modern dance, New York City–based Emily Andrews parlays that craft’s contrasting principles of line and weight, positive and negative space, into her photography work. The beautifully captured balancing acts have garnered the attention of AD, WSJ Magazine, The New York Times, and others.

Glassworks offers a kaleidoscopic moment in a moody dining room.

If you love the enviable homes of Athena Calderone—a.k.a. EyeSwoon—Jessica Antola is a name you need to know. Antola has captured Calderone’s Instagram-famous spaces, as well as countless others.

The minimalist Brooklyn apartment of Coco Romack and Mars Hobrecker.

Winnie Au’s photography brings out the color and personality in each space she so smartly captures, whether it’s a playful Palm Springs hotel, a boldly designed New York apartment, or the creative studios of artists and makers.

A dining room in Greenwich, Connecticut, designed by Alison Hammatt Home.

From Nantucket antiques to contemporary interiors, Jane Beiles approaches a room as a still life, balancing textures, shapes, and scale rather than letting one trophy piece steal the show. Based in Fairfield, Connecticut, she has photographed work by Gil Schafer, Katie Ridder, Stonefox, and Bennett Leifer.

Chloe Fineman’s West Village home, designed by Tali Roth.

Andrew Bui loves dynamic, expressive lighting and strives to create images with a timeless quality to them. He comes from two generations of award-winning restaurateurs, and his food photography is just as delectable as his interior shots.

Filmmaker ShawnLevy’s dining room in Manhattan, designed by AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent

Raised in Texas and now based in Brooklyn, Max Burkhalter doesn’t shy away from assignments in the Lone Star State, having shot projects like David Adjaye’s crystalline Ruby City contemporary art center. Still, Burkhalter reps hard for Brooklyn and has collaborated with brands including In Common With and Roll & Hill.

Inside a 19th-century Brooklyn town house renovated by Hatchet Design & Build.

Nicholas Calcott has worked on a variety of editorial, commercial, and self-assigned projects across topics including home and belonging, creativity, and the future. He’s of Arabic, Jewish, and British heritage and also speaks French, so he brings an international sensibility to assignments.

The daughter of an architect and a photographer, Anita Calero brings an artistic eye to her still-life photography, and is equally adept at shooting nature and interiors. A celebrated fine-art photographer as well, Calero works between home bases in New York, Colombia, and Miami, living her philosophy that beauty is everywhere and “nothing is ugly.”

Photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment in Brooklyn Heights

A regular contributor to AD, New York, and other publications, Seth Caplan documents spaces with a keen sense of presence, emphasizing warm tones and moody shadows. He loves a good portrait and also shoots images for homeware brands including Bed Threads, Framebridge, and Caraway Home.

Sean Davidson beautifully captures the stillness of an organically neutral interior.

A favorite of many AD100 and AD PRO Directory studios, Sean Davidson has translated his industrial design background into a successful career in photography, frequently working with top fashion brands and design publications alike.

Polished yet raw, Blaine Davis’s style and compositions result in interior shots and portraits that are crisp and authentic—not unlike the glossy pages of the magazines in which they appear. (Including AD, of course.)

A historic Fifth Avenue mansion, built by Stanford White.

A documentary background shapes Hayley Ellen Day’s interest in the relationship between people and their spaces. Her interiors range from ornate salons to playful bathrooms, with small details offering clues to the lives unfolding beyond the frame.

Inside a reimagined 19th-century farmhouse in Southampton, New York, designer Ariel Okin animates a historic New York refuge using color and character.

Donna Dotan’s obsession with clean lines and natural light is evident across her catalog of interior shoots, in which spaces are portrayed as sun-kissed and in dazzling color. Her work has graced the pages of all major design publications, including AD.

A New York City apartment for Casameu New York, styled by Rebecca Bartoshesky

Combining strong compositional elements with a sense of warmth and sensitivity, Pippa Drummond—a Kiwi photographer now based in New York City—has been commissioned by the likes of Dwell and Herman Miller.

Bovina Farm and Fermentory in New York’s Catskill Mountains.

Soft daylight and tactile finishes lend Sarah Elliott’s interiors an easy, unhurried feeling. Her photographs for Upstate invite a closer look at country living, while her work with Elizabeth Roberts, Nune, and others brings that intimacy to many homes.

A bedroom on the Upper East Side of New York, designed by The Interiors Concierge and styled by Pablo Olguin

Whether a space is minimalist or maximalist, Claire Esparros is able to distill its essence by amplifying the serenity or vibrancy of her photos. Framing spatial sequences and highlighting vignettes are among her strengths.

A landing in Kacey Musgraves’s Nashville home.

Lelanie Foster’s portraits of Serena Williams, Kacey Musgraves, and Misty Copeland for AD make the home as compelling as the person. For designers seeking photographs that introduce the inhabitants as well as the interiors, her portfolio merits a look.

A bedroom designed by Mieke ten Have and photographed by Frank Frances in New York’s Hudson Valley

Trained in art practice at the School of Visual Arts, photographer Frank Frances has contributed his versatile eye to AD, British Vogue, West Elm, and others. His photography, which expands beyond interiors into beauty, food, and fashion, has appeared in exhibitions at galleries across the world, including Sasha Wolf Gallery, the Studio Museum of Harlem, and Werkstadt Graz.

Kirsten Francis captures a collectors’ trove.

An NYC–based lifestyle photographer specializing in interiors and portraits, Kirsten Francis has shot sun-drenched spaces by a roster of designers including Ashley Darryl, Alyssa Kapito, and Emily C. Butler.

A family room in Park City, Utah, designed by Wendy Labrum Interiors.

If Athena Calderone’s coffee table book Live Beautiful has earned a permanent spot on your coffee table, you’re already acquainted with Nicole Franzen’s photography. The New York talent’s portfolio also spans hospitality and cookbooks, giving homebodies and hosts alike something to savor.

Inside a private home on the Amalfi Coast.

The skill with which Patrick Fraser is able to portray history and character in his images is captivating. Born in the UK and recently relocated to Connecticut from the West Coast, he often takes inspiration from objects, landscapes, and people that have been forgotten or ignored.

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

The photographer shot his own kitchen on Long Island.

Douglas Friedman gives elaborate interiors a sense of drama, using natural light to bring out their materials. Along with photographing sumptuous rooms by Ken Fulk, Nicole Hollis, and Kelly Wearstler, the photographer has welcomed AD into his own Marfa retreat.

Alice Gao’s lens has been known to linger in shadows, resulting in a photograph that can romanticize even the most neutral, pared-back interiors. Her style brings minimalist, modern settings—such as those of clients Yabu Pushelberg and Toast UK, among others—beautifully to life.

This Brooklyn-based creative has brought an expert eye to shoots in countless stylish homes, restaurants like Altro Paradiso, and the studios of talents like Trueing and Christian Siriano.

The sunlit living room of a townhouse in New York City’s West Village

His training as a painter informs Gaut’s portrait-like images of interiors, imbuing each space with personality. AD has published his images of New York apartments, ski chalets in Wyoming, and farmhouses in Nova Scotia, but he’s also a fine art photographer whose prints have appeared in stores including Design Within Reach.

Inside celeb stylist Kate Young’s upstate New York home.

Family life in all its facets is a frequent muse for William Geddes—his own wife and daughters included—though he’s also keen on assignments across the editorial, advertising, and publishing industries. A graduate of The New School, Parsons School for Design, Geddes also offers both simple and complex video shoots among his professional services.

A vignette from Elsa Perretti’s home in Spain

Adrianna Glaviano finds visual wit in the smallest arrangements, such as jewelry on striped straws, or personal effects gathered around a sink. Her still-life sensibility offers designers a way to make the objects within a room part of its story. Working between New York and Milan, she counts AD France, HAY, FLOS, and Gohar World among her clients.

An Upstate New York couple painstakingly restored this geometric 1970s hideaway.

Golden hour appears to be Nick Glimenakis’s choice time to shoot, when he’s able to capture the warm light, long shadows, and exaggerated contrasts that up the drama in his imagery.

An indoor-outdoor space designed by Mike Moser Studio.

Residential design and hospitality meet in Christian Harder’s portfolio, which includes work with Jake Arnold, Ash, and AvroKO. His photographs of Darren Jett’s Brooklyn apartment for AD offer a useful introduction to his eye for rooms with personality. He’s also kept up a fine art photography practice and is repped by OneWay Gallery in Providence and Narragansett, Rhode Island.

In a Malibu home designed by Lala Reimagined, a dining area is filled with bentwood and natural fiber delights.

Ori Harpaz’s sharp editorial style has landed him multiple features in all of the top design magazines. His eye for color and penchant for strict angles mean his images are bold, striking, and arresting.

A marble bathroom in a Finger Lakes estate designed by Jeremiah Brent.

Ethan Herrington’s career began in commercial still-life photography, and places and things get equal billing in his portfolio—welcome news for those who obsess over both the room and its contents. Based in Cold Spring, New York, he has worked with Billy Cotton, Commune, and Studio Dorion.

A sunken living room oozes cool in this airy abode.

Formerly a fashion and textile print designer, Angela Hau—who operates out of San Francisco and NYC—has adapted her keen understanding of shape, scale, and balance to photography. Industry brands Thompson Street Studio, Egg Collective, and more have tapped Hau to beautifully capture interiors and product photography.

Studio Valle de Valle transformed a historic home in Toronto.

Jenni Kayne’s Los Angeles home and Neal Beckstedt’s wood-clad Chelsea apartment have both met Stephen Kent Johnson’s lens. He favors intimate views and revealing details over an all-encompassing wide angle, complete with soft light and carefully framed vignettes.

Inside a renovated California cabin with interiors designed by Fritz Haeg and Jeremy Schipper.

Recently relocated from LA, André Jones brings a sunny and warm approach to architecture and lifestyle photography. From rustic home interiors to sleek corporate buildings, his images are consistently well-framed and proportioned.

The living room in Walton Goggins’s home in New York’s Hudson Valley

The grand Victorian, simple Colonial, and traditional farmhouse-style homes scattered across upstate New York are a common subject for Kate Jordan’s lens. Her shots of Shaker-style kitchens and cozy living rooms depict all the warmth and familiarity they were designed to exude.

Join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Learn more

The city takes center stage in this New York apartment.

Long shadows and glimpses through windows give Joseph Kramm’s interiors a palpable sense of depth. His work with galleries including The Future Perfect and Hostler Burrows also makes him well versed in giving collectible furniture its moment.

One of the most versatile interior photographers in the Northeast, Jared Kuzia captures residential projects up and down the Eastern Seaboard for architects, interior designers, and publications. Whether shooting urban apartments or coastal cabins, he is motivated by “conveying the essence of home,” as he puts it.

A bedroom in Isabella Rosselini’s converted barn on Long Island by architect Pietro Cicognani.

Francesco Lagnese’s interiors work moves comfortably between a spare, sunlit corner and the layered rooms of Tom Scheerer, Williams Lawrence, and Veere Grenney. Working between New York, Palm Beach, and all over Europe from his base in Munich, his itinerary extends well beyond the living room, as he also shoots architecture, portraits, and travel.

With an instantly recognizable, highly atmospheric style that’s won favor with top designers and stylists, William Jess Laird is consistently in high demand. His calm, minimal photos appear regularly in AD and many other leading art and design publications.

People are part of the picture in David Land’s photographs, from children playing in a living room to a family gathered on the sofa. In his images of work by Danielle Colding, Nina Barnieh-Blair, and more, color and everyday activity make these interiors feel welcoming, with life happening inside them.

A high-contrast interior captured by Heami Lee

There’s something innately playful about the images Lee captures for clients. Whether shooting still lifes for Edie Parker or Design Within Reach, Brooklyn-based Lee creates work that is undeniably cool.

Tour a Josh Greene–designed Upper East Side family home with a tented room

Capturing lived-in interiors in an authentically stunning demeanor is Tim Lenz’s calling card. The talent has shot the work of AD100 studio Carrier and Company, Hendricks Churchill, and Augusta Hoffman.

A den on the top floor of a home in Provincetown, Massachusetts, designed by Stanton Schwartz Design Group.

Consider Sean Litchfield’s portfolio a love letter to New England. Maine lake houses, Cape Cod cottages, and Boston brownstones—his portfolio makes room for both rustic intimacy and a more polished setting with Nina Campbell, Patrick Ahearn, and Erin Gates included.

The dining room in Rachel Brosnahan’s apartment, which the actress designed with Zoë Feldman.

Pernille Loof’s restrained compositions give texture, color, and shadow room to register. A minimalist sensibility runs through her interiors and still lifes, bringing a crispness to the frame without stripping away the warmth of the subject.

A living room in Birmingham, Alabama, by Georgette Sturam Design

Adam Kane Macchia’s balanced room views keep architectural features clearly legible, highlighting everything from ceiling beams to the rhythm of tall windows. His portfolio is particularly useful for designers seeking photographs that show how furnishings and a home’s bones work together.

Meghan Marin photographs residential spaces as she finds them: unmade beds, displays of collected items, tables laid for dinner—all the idiosyncrasies of which bring rawness and authenticity to her shots, even if they’ve been styled to appear that way.

Step inside Nate Berkus and Jeremiah Brent’s freshly renovated Fifth Avenue family home

If the name Kelly Marshall isn’t immediately familiar, surely her contrast-rich photography—seen regularly in the pages of AD—will ring a bell. Marshall, who’s a member of the Female Design Council as well as the Black Artists + Designers Guild, is based in New York.

Designer Sara Story’s New York City living room

Joshua McHugh’s interests extend from private residences to museums and artists’ historic homes, including those of Carlo Mollino and Wharton Esherick. His portfolio is an appealing resource for designers whose interiors put architecture, art, and objects in conversation.

Creative dream team Murdock Solon Architects and designer David Cafiero lovingly injected whimsy and joy across all four floors of a New York City family home.

A cover star, Read McKendree’s lively interiors have fronted issues of Elle Decoration Germany, House Beautiful, and Luxe, as well as catalogs for Serena & Lily. We also love his portraits of artists at work in their studios.

Inside a Minneapolis home decadently designed by Prospect Refuge Studio.

Chris Mottalini’s aim each time he photographs a home is to create a portrait of the space and its occupants, revealing what’s hidden beneath the surface. His recent projects include the photography for interior designer Nina Freudenberger’s book Mountain House.

A loggia in the Moroccan home of writer and gardener Umberto Pasti.

Ngoc Minh Ngo’s images of gardens feel enveloping, with layered foliage and paths that draw the eye into the landscape. The New York photographer and author’s botanical photography brings the same attention to a single bloom, making her a natural fit for projects where planting matters. In her images of landscapes by Miranda Brooks and Dan Pearson, every leaf feels considered.

Tour fashion designer Adam Lippes’s bucolic Berkshires home

Growing up around creative matriarchs—her mother a weaver and her grandmother a painter—Isabel Parra understands the importance of an artisan’s tool kit. Her devices of choice? Natural light and its emotive shadow play and honest interior compositions. No wonder she’s caught the attention of fashion designer Adam Lippes, Oomph Home, House & Garden UK, AD, and others.

Natural light, analogue photography, and a sense of intimate nostalgia guide Clément Pascal’s work—with vintage cars making occasional cameos. French-born and now based in New York, his design photographs often keep people in the picture, conveying how a room is occupied as readily as the objects that furnish it.

A home in Sag Harbor Bay by BMA Architects with interior design by The Unionworks.

Trained in interior architecture, Eric Petschek pairs careful attention to design details with a notably calm atmosphere, as shown in his images of Worrell Yeung’s Hudson Valley home for AD. His softly lit, precise compositions give even a spare room emotional weight, without letting its architectural logic disappear.

The view from Kelly Behun’s Manhattan apartment.

Working across New York and Europe, Richard Powers has an eye for architecture’s graphic possibilities: a railing’s shadow, a curved volume, a building set against open sky. In his images, the relationship between form, light, and setting is central to a project.

Working out of New York and Paris, Arrow (Sharon) Radisch’s clients include luxury brands like Gucci and Chanel, as well as editorial outlets like Cereal, for whom she shot Le Corbusier’s Paris apartment.

Inside an AD digital editor’s light-filled Maine abode

Tara Rice takes a photo-journalistic approach to her work, whether in the forests or on the shorelines of Maine or across the far-reaching corners of the world. Her photography is fueled by curiosity about people and places, and the varied ways in which they overlap.

An alum of the School of Visual Arts’s photography program, Brooklyn-based Rayon Richards has 20 years of professional experience, with clients ranging from Def Jam to Fortune. Though accomplished in many arenas—he also paints and plays the drums—we’re especially taken by his eye for vibrant color photography.

Portrait of ceramicist and painter Woody De Othello

A creative producer, curator, and photographer, Kameron Richie has partnered with Nike, VSCO, Floyd, and Everlane on a range of projects. His interior shots—light-dappled and a tinge nostalgic—offer an inviting glimpse inside the lives of his subjects. Richie, who hails from Texas, now holds court in New York City.

An apartment in Casa Ramos, a 1906 apartment building in Barcelona.

New York. Los Angeles. Mexico City. Barcelona. Pia Riverola’s work locales read like a very appealing itinerary. Her sensitivity to color and passing light gives her photographs a dreamy, nostalgic pull. Interiors sit within a wider world of landscapes and everyday encounters, making her work especially appealing when a project’s sense of place matters.

Limewash paint brings emotion to an otherwise quiet interior

Life and movement appear in full focus throughout the varied portfolio of Julia Robbs, whose work in fashion and beauty photography naturally translates over to interiors. The lifestyle component of the home, and how its occupants use it, is key to her vibrant aesthetic.

A seating area in Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s home in North Carolina

A beloved portraitist, Reid Rolls started his career shooting album covers for record labels. The California native, who now lives in Brooklyn, also photographs fashion, travel, ad campaigns, and, of course, interiors, including his atmospheric images of Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s home in Charlotte for AD.

An aquatic-themed bathroom in an 1840s townhouse in Brooklyn, New York, designed by Charlap Hyman & Herrero with murals and mosaics by Lukas Geronimas Giniotis and Allison Eden Studios.

Jason Schmidt is as interested in creative people as the spaces they shape. His portraits of artists at work and photographs of buildings such as Frank Gehry’s Santa Monica home offer designers a perspective rooted in the arts.

Inside actor John Leguizamo’s New York City brownstone, on which he and his wife collaborated with myriad design creatives, namely, Barbara Batesko, Nathan Turner, Lucien Rees Roberts, Leslie Rylee, and Harry Gutfreund.

From established businesses to young brands, Tori Sikkema will not only photograph your projects, she’ll also support your branding through consultations that will tailor her shoots to meet specific needs and goals. Her aim is always to allow her clients’ design style to shine through while creating photographs that evoke a sense of place and feeling.

The Connecticut living room of Matthew Malin and Andrew Goetz

Having shot the likes of Maude Apatow, Malene Barnett, and Michael Imperioli for AD, Calcutta-born Ashok Sinha’s portfolio of architecture, interiors, and portraits also includes The New York Times, Bloomberg, and several other distinguished outlets.

A primary suite in Brooklyn designed by Young Huh.

Jacob Snavely’s interiors photographs give lofty ceilings and carefully planned sightlines their due, with clear views that explain a room’s layout. His still-life and portrait work offers designers a way to extend that story beyond the overall space.

A living room featuring a rug designed by Colin King for Beni Rugs.

Billal Taright’s eye gravitates toward sculptural objects, spare arrangements, and the space around them. Warm tones and considered framing lend even a shelf or mantel quiet presence. The New York photographer moves between interiors, fashion, and collectible design, with Ralph Lauren Home, Colin King, and Luke Edward Hall also among his clients.

A kitchen by Jenna Chused of Chused and Co. for Isla Porter’s Tastemakers series.

Christian Torres makes interiors feel inviting and lived in, drawing on a practice that also spans hospitality and travel. He can participate from concept and location scouting through styling and lighting, helping designers carry a cohesive idea through the shoot.

Pattern and pigment freshen a traditional sitting room

No design detail is lost on Lesley Unruh, a Tennessee native and alum of Domino. Unruh, who now lives in New York City, has worked with Anna Burke Interiors, Malene Barnett, and CeCe Barfield Thompson, among others.

The grand staircase in a historic Georgian home in Pennsylvania designed by Haldon House.

Jason Varney brings a painterly handling of light and a strong feel for color to restaurants, hotels, and homes. His food photography makes him particularly useful for hospitality projects where the atmosphere extends from the dining room to the table, but homes are always on the menu too.

An indoor/outdoor living area in Sag Harbor, designed by Garnett.DePasquale Projects.

Nicholas Venezia brings architectural training and eight years at Selldorf Architects to his photography. His process connects a project’s underlying ideas with its visual story, a valuable trait when a designer wants the photographs to communicate more than appearances.

A 1909 mansion in New Jersey belonging to director Ruben Fleischer, designed by Studio DB.

If Brooklyn brownstones and beautifully considered hotels populate your design daydreams, spend some time with Matthew Williams’s portfolio. His interiors photography moves between whole-room views and studies of furniture, materials, and smaller objects. His portfolio includes homes by Elizabeth Roberts and Studio DB, giving designers examples of how a project can unfold across a sequence of images.

Tour a strikingly modern home in East Hampton

A resident of New York City but available for work worldwide, Tim Williams captures a sense of life in his photographs of commercial and residential interiors. His images recently graced AD PRO’s coverage of David Thomas’s new Madison Avenue outpost for Manolo Blahnik.

The powder room of a West Village townhouse designed by Starrett Ringbom.

A veteran of the fashion industry, Regan Wood shifted her focus to architecture and interior photography some time ago. Still, she sees a connection between them in that both form an “outward expression of one’s inner life.”

#4796. I Found the 11 Best Running Shoes for Women for Every Type of Run

From trail running to marathons to daily training, our running shoe guide has a recommendation for every runner.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

LOW-IMPACT EXERCISES might be forever buzzy, but the running community is going stronger than ever. From 5Ks to marathons, lots of women are lacing up to go for a run and getting all the physical and mental health benefits that come with it. Data suggests running is great for everything from cardiovascular fitness to a healthier mindset, and it may even lower your risk of eight major diseases, making it a solid fitness habit to get into. And then there’s the fact that running makes you feel like you’ve accomplished something amazing (because you have).

As a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too. The best running shoes for women provide support and cushioning, with the perfect level of fit to help you forget about your footwear while you run.

While you can skimp on some fitness gear, a quality pair of running shoes is an important investment, according to Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois “I am very much in the camp of paying for a really good pair of running shoes,” she says. “It can help really minimize injury in the future.” (Still, if you’re on a tight budget or just want to save a buck, these are our favorite cheap running shoes.)

But, before taking the plunge on racking up miles, it’s important to figure out what kind of heel-to-toe drop, toe box, stability, cushioning, and heel stack is best for you. Finding the perfect running shoes involves understanding how specific design elements impact your comfort, performance, and overall experience.

There is no right or wrong, as everyone has different needs (and those needs for running shoes differ from walking shoes), but we'll go over the most important factors to consider when shopping for running shoes.

Hoka does it right when it comes to a durable, high-quality shoe—specifically the Clifton 11, which was released in July 2026 in tandem with the higher-performance-oriented Clifton Pro. The Clifton family has been a crowd pleaser in the running community and amongst WH editors for a long time, and with good reason.

The Clifton 11 is considered one of the brand’s most versatile running shoes, making it a good fit for everyone from beginners to seasoned pros. WH style editor Shannon Zitz says her feet never felt fatigued while she was testing this shoe, even with plantar fasciitis. “There’s technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely noticed it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running,” she says.

The Clifton 11 has an eight-millimeter heel-to-toe drop to help alleviate pressure on the plantar fascia, and the brand shaved off almost half an ounce from the weight of the model’s previous version, the Clifton 10, primarily through weight-saving revisions to the shoe’s upper. This was the primary change, with Hoka keeping the midsole that we know and love the same.

These shoes offer maximum cushioning you’ll feel—the same EVA foam found in the Bondi 9 without the extra bulk. Just be aware that these don’t offer any stability innovations for flat feet, which is especially essential if you’re prone to overpronation. As for fit, the toe box does run narrow, but luckily, wide sizing is available.

Read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro

On has built an empire out of its highly cushioned Cloudmonster line. But its most cushioned shoe of all is the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, an impressively bouncy sneaker that’ll make you feel like a gazelle bounding down the street.

It’s generally accepted that the more cushioning a shoe has, the heavier its weight (because of all that foam packed into the midsole). But the On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper manages to deliver a highly cushioned shoe in a relatively lightweight 7.5 oz package. The result is a next-level energy return that feels like it’s propelling you forward with each step.

This sneaker has a soft, breathable upper to minimize foot sweat, along with a highly padded heel collar that lowers the risk of rubbing. I’ve worn a lot of running shoes, and that heel collar may be the thickest I’ve ever seen. There’s a nice, roomy toe box, too.

While there’s a lot to love about the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, it’s not perfect. This shoe’s $220 price tag puts it out of reach for many, and the tongue is on the thin side (not a deal-breaker, but some people prefer something more padded). Still, if you have the budget for it and like to feel like you’re running on actual clouds, this is a solid choice.

Think of a daily trainer as the chameleon of the running shoe world. This sneaker needs to be able to be durable enough for regular use, comfortable, and versatile enough to handle higher mileage along with speedier runs. The Adidas Adizero Evo SL was designed with all of that in mind, serving up a highly adaptable shoe that works for nearly everyone. That’s probably why this shoe keeps landing on the feet of runners all over the place.

The Adizero Evo SL has a soft, bouncy feel underfoot and plenty of energy return thanks to Adidas’ proprietary Lightstrike Pro foam packed into the midsole. It’s also relatively lightweight, clocking in at just under 8 oz. The shoe’s peppy sensation and slight rocker shape support your stride but don’t push you forward in a way that feels unnatural.

This sneaker has an engineered mesh upper to let your feet breathe, even when you’re clocking some serious mileage. This shoe has a slightly tapered toe box, which isn’t for everyone. The outsole is also a little flat and isn’t the grippiest you’ll find, but road runners are unlikely to have an issue. While you’re probably not choosing a running shoe based on looks alone, it doesn’t hurt that the Adizero Evo SL looks sleek.

The best shoe for recovery runs is a total workhorse, delivering enough stability and cushioning to keep you comfortable as you move along at a moderate pace. The Brooks Ghost Max 3 is up for the challenge, with a wide, stable base and supportive feel to take the pressure off your joints.

This isn’t a stability shoe, per se—it won’t work to correct your stride—but it still creates a sense like you’re not going to roll an ankle or have any other gait issues as you pound the pavement. The Ghost Max 3 is a heavier shoe, although I haven’t noticed any fatigue or extra drag in it. But this sneaker holds up well to high-volume running. I wear this regularly and have never noticed any durability issues.

The Ghost Max 3 features nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam for support and cushioning. However, it won’t give you a sinking-in feel and there is limited energy return, which could be a pro or con, depending on what you’re after. This sneaker also has a jacquard mesh upper that feels a little softer than many other running shoes out there. The Ghost Max 3 provides plenty of room, from the midfoot to the toe box, making it a good fit for people with wider feet. Just don’t plan to do any speed work in this shoe—it’s a little too heavy for that.

It's clear that Lululemon’s Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There’s a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you’re going down.

Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that’s pretty common in a trail shoe, and it got better with time and more wear.

There’s a wide range of shoes that consider themselves “stability” sneakers, but the Hoka Arahi 8 does a solid job correcting your stride with each step without being annoying. Many stability shoes are clunky and heavy, but the Arahi 8 manages to be lightweight at just 7.7 oz.

The Arahi 8 features a lot of changes from the previous version, the Arahi 7. This shoe uses special H-frame technology, featuring foam at the inner and outer foot, to deliver a more balanced support system. It’s roomy and comfortable, too. But this shoe is clearly not for everyone.

The level of stability is high, and that constant gait correction may feel like too much for some people. It also isn’t very responsive, so you’re not getting much back from your shoe with each stride other than security. (To be fair, though, that’s what people are usually after with a stability shoe.) Still, the Arahi 8 is impressively cushioned and very comfortable, whether you’re working your way through a long training session or just going out on a daily run.

Long runs require plenty of cushioning to support you along the way. The Nike Vomero Plus, which won the award for Best Cushioned Running Shoe in the 2026 Women’s Health Fitness Awards, is here to help. This shoe delivers a fun, bouncy feel that helps propel you as you rack up the miles.

The Vomero Plus has a roomy toe box and overall comfortable feel, serving up a shoe that makes long runs a little more seamless. That bounciness comes courtesy of Nike’s ZoomX foam, which is positioned along the length of the shoe. The engineered upper is crafted from yarn for a soft, breathable sensation.

The Vomero Plus provides a grippy outsole, making it perfect for the pavement. But if you’re looking for a stability shoe, the Vomero Plus isn’t it. Its high heel stack and bounciness is too much for that. But if you want a highly cushioned feel as you log some serious miles, this is an excellent choice.

The right race day shoe has the tough challenge of being supportive, cushiony, and lightweight, helping you to hit a PR without feeling like your footwear is holding you back. The New Balance FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5 is designed with longer-distance racers (think: half and marathon runners) in mind, but can still be an excellent choice for 5Ks and 10Ks thanks to its lightweight (6 oz) construction and solid energy return.

Let’s get this out of the way now: At $265, this is not a cheap shoe. With that, it’s unlikely to be a good investment for the occasional racer. But if your weekends are booked with road races, it’s worth at least considering.

This shoe delivers a locked-in feel, along with great traction to give you more confidence, even over wet surfaces. The roomy toe box and breathable upper also reinforce the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5’s comfortable feel. This shoe is stable without sacrificing punchiness, helping you to feel supported as you stride. Just be aware that the midfoot and heel may feel a little too narrow for those with wider feet. But, luckily, this sneaker is available in wide widths, too.

Read More: Best Running Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis

The lululemon Beyondfeel running shoes truly live up to their name. They’re comfortable at the heels (and everywhere), with a heel stack that provides just the right amount of cushioning. It absorbs impact while still feeling responsive, especially during long runs. Plus, the cushioning around the ankle delivers security in every step.

The heel-to-toe drop is also a game changer—it really makes a difference for runners who heel-strike. Instead of feeling the usual jarring sensation from heel-striking, there are smooth transitions from each step. The bounce in the heel also makes it easier to maintain a steady stride without losing momentum, which is a huge benefit for runners who naturally land on their heels. The shoes guide feet to strike with the midfoot instead of the heel.

These shoes feel slightly bouncy while you run, and offer decent grip for trails and roads, making for a versatile running shoe. If you’re an overpronator, this isn’t the shoe for you—it doesn’t provide enough medial support (on the inside of the shoe). But it’s got plenty of features to make running a dream for heel strikers.

There’s a range in severity with overpronators, and what works for one won’t work for everyone. But the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 does a solid job trying to please everyone in the overpronation camp. This shoe delivers a feel that’s not too soft or too firm, giving you the support and stability you need without feeling like you’re in a “special” shoe.

This shoe is lightweight for a stability shoe at 8.5 oz, making it good for most runs that don’t involve speed work. It also delivers a solid, locked-in sensation to make you feel secure with each step. The shoe’s OrthoLite sockliner also supports that cozier feel. The Gel-Nimbus 28 feels slightly springy underfoot, which is rare for a stability shoe. (Still, the overall effect isn’t very responsive compared to non-stability shoes.)

Asics in general tends to run narrow and the Gel-Nimbus 28 is no exception. If your feet tend to teeter between regular and wide sizes, you may want to consider hedging your bets and trying out a larger size.

The best shoe for speed work is very different from what you need for distance training or even race day. The Saucony Endorphin Azura is a lightweight (7.5 oz) shoe with a snappy feel that still manages to make you feel stable and locked in as you zip around.

The Saucony Endorphin Azura uses Pebax foam to create a responsive, bouncy feel, making you feel a little faster than usual. It also has a wide and stable base for added security during training. While it’s designed for speed, you can still comfortably wear this sneaker for longer runs and daily mileage. Just be aware that the shoe’s special SpeedRoll technology may feel slightly awkward at slower speeds.

The Endorphin Azura’s outsole features XT-900 rubber for a grippy feel underfoot, making you feel comfortable pushing the pace. Saucony shoes are known for a narrower fit, and the Endorphin Azura is no exception. If you have wider feet, it may be best to look elsewhere. (It unfortunately doesn’t come in wide sizes.)

Maximum Cushioning: This type of cushion feels amazingly plush and has excellent shock absorption, which is essential for long-distance running. While they’re designed to minimize the impact on the joints, they’re not the best for speed workouts unless the shoe has a lower heel-to-toe drop and some firmness.

Medium: If you want to balance speed with stability, medium cushioning is ideal. Too much cushioning can cause runners with flat feet to overpronate more from the bulkiness and softness. So, this type of cushioning is best if you want a more aligned gait.

This is the difference in height between the heel and front part (known as the forefoot) of the shoe. It can impact how your foot lands on the ground when you run. Low drops (0 to 4 mm) are flatter and encourage a natural running style where you land in the middle or front of your foot. They’re great if you like to feel close to the ground, enjoy trail running, or prefer a minimalist shoe design. Medium drop (5 to 8 mm) is a versatile option that offers mid-height and cushioning—this works well for most running styles. High drop (9 to 12 mm) tends to have more height in the heel to absorb impact (this is great for heel-strikers).

This is the height of the cushion under the heel. It’s measured from the outsole (the bottom of the shoe) to the insole (where your foot rests). Higher stacks offer more softness for long-distance running or for those who need less impact on the joints. Prioritizing this means sacrificing ground feel, and for some, that may feel unbalanced given the additional height.

Running shoes can provide a slew of benefits to suit your feet, but podiatrists stress the importance of getting a well-fitting shoe. “The shoe should fit your foot well and not cause any rubbing on the toes,” says Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California “They should feel comfortable immediately upon putting them on and walking around.”

Consider these areas of the shoe when checking the fit:

Toe Box: This is the front part of the shoe where the toes sit. Toes spread naturally when you have extra room in the toe box, and this is especially important during long runs since feet can swell. But if the toe box is too big, it can lead to sliding and instability in the shoes.

Length: Since feet often swell from pounding pavement, it’s a good idea to have about a thumb’s width away from the tip of the shoe to your toe. If you’re unsure of your size, the best bet is to visit a running store to get properly fitted.

Arch Support: Those with flat feet and overpronators (when your foot lands on your outside heel and rolls inward) will want to look for shoes with enough firmness and high arch support to help keep feet aligned. Too much cushioning can create an unbalanced feeling, which can further aggravate pain. Those with neutral to high arches will have no issues wearing shoes with neutral support. Most shoes specify which arch type they accommodate, so make sure to read their product descriptions. And, definitely don’t wear shoes with no arch support—your feet need support.

The type of running workouts you plan to do will dictate elements like cushioning, support, and weight. More cushioning is often better with daily training and distance runs. You may also get away with a slightly heavier (but not too heavy) shoe, which usually means there’s more cushioning and stability. But shoes for speed work and race day tend to have less cushioning and a lighter weight, making it easier to move faster. For a deep-dive into the topic of running shoe selection, check out our story about how to figure out which type of running shoe you need.

A stability shoe can help correct gait issues like overpronation, which is when your foot rolls inward excessively when you run or walk. Not everyone needs a stability shoe, but some level of stability is important for reducing injury risk when you’re an overpronator. There are a few ways to tell if you overpronate, per Graves: Your feet appear to be rolling inward when you stand in a relaxed position and the heels of shoes you’ve worn are tilted inward.

You should switch out your running shoes every 300 to 500 miles. An easy way to maximize your shoe lifespan is to have a few pairs that you rotate between runs. Also, if you visually see them degrading, it's time to snag a new pair.

Running shoes can be washed in cold water in the washing machine with light detergent, or spot-cleaned with a sponge. But, you should never put your shoes in the dryer—they can shrink! Instead, let them air dry in the sun.

A simple at-home way to determine your arch type is the wet footprint test. You simply dip your foot in the water and step onto paper. If you see your entire foot, you have flat feet. Your foot will look like a comma if you have high arches, while a neutral arch will show slight elevation.

I’ve tested dozens of pairs of running shoes to determine which make the cut for the best running shoes for women. As a personal trainer, fitness writer, and runner with years of experience testing running shoes, I put each pair to the test during two-mile runs where I evaluated key performance factors such as cushioning, stability, comfort, support, traction, and responsiveness. I also considered how well the shoes supported my stride and whether or not they helped me maintain a consistent pace. Additionally, WH fitness editors provided feedback on select shoes they love to wear during training and racing.

#4795. Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Jensen Huang did not unveil a breakthrough chip on Monday. He simply got his old job back—and Nvidia shares surged more than 30%, while the Nasdaq jumped nearly 7% in midday trading.

The reaction revealed something more consequential than Wall Street’s fondness for a charismatic CEO: investors had spent 11 days confronting how much of the AI boom runs through one person.

Huang, who resigned November 12 amid revelations about extramarital affairs and an unproven Chinese espionage allegation involving a former customer executive, has returned as CEO, president, and director.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Nvidia’s board says his reinstatement poses no national security risk, based partly on input from senior U.S. officials. Its independent investigation, however, is not over.

The company did not stop making chips. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO, Harvey Jones took over as Nvidia’s first board chairman, and executives insisted the technology roadmap and customer commitments remained intact.

Kress presided over earnings that showed roughly $116 billion in quarterly sales and projected about $130 billion for the following quarter—staggering numbers that still failed to calm the market.

Inside Nvidia, the transition looked considerably less routine. During the first companywide meeting without Huang, staff had submitted about 700 questions, many concerning compensation and board transparency.

Kress promised pay increases and extra stock awards in December, months earlier than planned. Executives took turns assuring workers that the company could serve customers without Huang; some employees nevertheless discussed leaving if his absence became permanent.

The pushback extended outside headquarters. An online petition gathered roughly 200,000 names, though signers’ claimed employee or shareholder affiliations were not independently verified. Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, whose firms had disclosed about $2.1 billion in Nvidia shares, urged a deliberate succession process that kept Huang’s return possible. It was an unusual message to directors searching for a replacement: don't rush to replace the founder.

This letter was sent to Nvidia's board today.

Absolutely share @altcap belief that this letter outlines minimum acceptable standards. pic.twitter.com/ST2f5TMAa1

— Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) November 14, 2026

In other words, Nvidia couldn’t survive the scandal—not the one about Huang cheating, but the one about Huang leaving.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and turned graphics processors into the hardware behind modern AI. But his power also lies in the relationships surrounding those chips: cloud giants buying entire data centers of GPUs, developers locked into Nvidia’s CUDA software, suppliers building its next systems and policymakers deciding which markets it can serve.

Reuters reports that he has overseen roughly 60 direct reports and personally shaped major deals and product decisions.

He has also become a financier and ambassador for the AI ecosystem. Nvidia has invested in companies including CoreWeave and Nebius, which buy computing hardware to rent AI capacity to others.

That web of investment, sales, and financing is precisely why his disappearance unnerved markets far beyond Nvidia. After his outsting, Chinese customers delayed or canceled orders while leadership was unsettled; the whole Nasdaq index and the wider S&P500 crashed and odds for a bubble pop spiked to more than 70% on prediction markets.

Then, on Monday, minutes after his return, CoreWeave and Nebius shares each jumped more than 20% alongside Nvidia which had its best day in history—Huang also probably had his best day ever, too.

To have a grasp of Huang’s influence, one just needs to follow the money.

Elon Musk backed the reinstatement campaign; Y Combinator chief Garry Tan and Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney were among other prominent supporters. Bill Ackman celebrated Monday with “sanity prevails.” Trump pressed the case personally, later saying his intervention was “very important” and that the administration assured directors there was no national security obstacle to Huang’s return.

That backing helps explain the whiplash: On November 17, Jones said the board would not reinstate Huang, citing conduct inconsistent with Nvidia’s standards. Six days later, the same directors voted unanimously to bring him back. They say meetings satisfied them about his candor and leadership, but have not explained exactly what changed. Supporters see recognition of an indispensable founder; critics see a board yielding to powerful outsiders.

Bullish analysts argue that restoring Huang reduces execution and talent-retention risk. Dan Ives has framed Nvidia as a $300 stock with Huang versus $225 without him, while Melius Research upgraded the shares to “buy” with a $220 target.

Yet Monday’s roughly 30%-plus rebound followed a Friday close of $125.53; even near $165, Nvidia remains well below its October peak. Buying the comeback means paying much more for the same projected chip sales.

The other side is harder to price. Michael Burry criticized the reversal, and legal scrutiny of Huang, Nvidia’s export controls and its board continues. The company is establishing a board committee for national security and export-control oversight and recruiting a chief compliance officer.

None of that resolves the fundamental AI question: whether customers can earn enough on massive infrastructure spending to sustain Nvidia’s growth.

Huang’s return repairs a missing link between Nvidia, its customers, Wall Street, and Washington. The 11-day crisis showed how much confidence that link carries—and how vulnerable the AI trade becomes when it breaks.

What he has not yet won back is an unquestioned mandate to lead.

#4794. Cross River Bank enters Bitcoin-backed lending with $250K loans

The US bank is offering Bitcoin-backed loans ranging from $10,000 to $250,000 through LendingUSA, allowing borrowers to access cash without selling their holdings.

Cross River Bank and consumer financing company LendingUSA have launched a Bitcoin-backed lending program offering loans of up to $250,000, allowing eligible borrowers to access funds without selling their Bitcoin holdings.

According to a Monday announcement, borrowers can take out loans ranging from $10,000 to $250,000, using their Bitcoin (BTC) as collateral. They can borrow 30%, 50% or 70% of the value of their coins, depending on the loan terms. Eligible borrowers can either make interest-only payments during the loan term or postpone payments until the loan is due.

However, the loans carry risks if Bitcoin’s price falls. Borrowers could be required to provide additional collateral or repay part of their loans, with pledged Bitcoin subject to liquidation if collateral requirements are not met.

Bitcoin traded at $62,788 as of 4:13 p.m. UTC on Monday, up 3.03% over the past 24 hours but down 28.20% year-to-date, according to TradingView data.

The partnership marks Cross River’s first Bitcoin-backed lending program as a loan originator. Bitcoin pledged as collateral will be held by a qualified third-party custodian throughout the loan term.

Other Bitcoin-backed lenders include Ledn, which has offered crypto-backed loans since 2018, and Coinbase, which introduced Bitcoin-backed loans through Morpho in January 2025. US banks are also involved, including Column N.A., which originates some loans offered through Strike, and Fortis Bank, which participates in commercial lending arrangements with Unchained.

#4793. 45 AD-Approved International Interior Photographers to Know for Your Next Project Abroad

They jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Read on to discover top talents working in Europe, Asia, Oceania, North Africa, South America, and Canada.

Born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and currently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography. His images often center around the collected objects that make a space personal and give it life.

A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.

With Harry Nuriev, Festen, and Bernard Dubois among his collaborators, Ludovic Balay is no stranger to interiors with a point of view. The Paris photographer’s roster also includes Halleroed, adding another distinctive design voice to the picture.

The drawing room of a Notting Hill home designed by Olivia Williams.

Henry Bourne’s photographs open a window into creative people’s private worlds. The UK photographer’s interiors and portrait work includes subjects such as John Pawson, Faye Toogood, Luca Guadagnino, and Rose Uniacke.

A London townhouse designed by AD100 designer Leonora Hamill

Helen Cathcart brings a painterly, atmospheric quality to her work, which has resonated with some of the world’s hottest brands, designers, and publications. Cathcart’s photos of interiors, in particular, proffer serenity and calm through their tonality.

The Row, Lemaire, and a host of AD interiors: François Coquerel’s portfolio is in very good company. The Paris photographer moves between fashion and design, with Massimo Adario and Oitoemponto among his architectural collaborators.

Designer Luca Cipelletti delivers architectural precision and material opulence to an art collector’s Porta Nuova apartment.

Partners in life and work, Michael Depasquale and Martina Maffini count industry names like Dimore Studio, Nilufar Gallery, and JW Anderson among their clients. The duo splits their time between Paris and Milan and injects dynamism into each shoot that becomes evident in the final, glossy-ready results.

A villa in New Zealand by Patterson Associates.

Simon Devitt doesn’t stop at photographing architecture: fine art photo books, exhibitions, and workshops also fill his calendar. Based in Wellington, he has worked with Fearon Hay, Shigeru Ban, and Olson Kundig, documenting buildings across New Zealand and beyond.

Joseph Dirand designs rooms; his brother Adrien photographs them, including the architect’s Paris apartment for AD. Also based in Paris, Adrien contributed photography to the book Joseph Dirand Interior. A creative family, to say the least.

Inside the Paris headquarters of ACNE studios

Having started his career in fashion, Dol Maillot is as beloved for his street style shots and travel photography as he is for his interiors. Born in the South of France, the globetrotting artist now lives in Paris.

A Kelly Behun apartment at London’s Whiteley hotel is just one reason to linger over Veerle Evens’s portfolio. The London photographer moves between interiors, food, and travel, with HBA Residential, Owl Design, and Christian Bense among her collaborators.

A color-drenched home in the Canary Islands.

Some interiors tell you as much about their owners as a portrait might. Miguel Flores-Vianna seeks out those personal worlds, bringing his curiosity not just to interiors but also to his books, including Haute Bohemians and Haute Bohemians Greece. Armchair travelers, settle in.

Join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Learn more

Inside the Paris apartment of Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, as seen in AD France.

Among international interior photographers, Jérôme Galland ups the ante with his photos through a combination of striking contrasts, dramatic angles, and an appreciation of scale. French châteaus, Italian palazzos, and Greek villas all appear at their most grand through his lens.

Venetian interiors and Moroccan retreats make tempting subjects: Kasia Gatkowska’s portfolio travels well. The Amsterdam-based photographer has worked with Vincenzo De Cotiis, Vincent Van Duysen, Axel Vervoordt, and Massimo Adario, among others.

The home of the ABC Concept founders in Karuizawa, Japan.

Kenzo Takada’s Paris home is just one stop in Mitchell Geng’s portfolio. The Tokyo photographer also captured a colorful Hong Kong residence for Vogue Hong Kong and includes architecture, interiors, and hospitality in his photographic itinerary.

Film buffs may recognize Luca Guadagnino, the Italian director, producer, and screenwriter behind films such as Call Me By Your Name; design lovers will know his interiors too. Milan photographer Giulio Ghirardi has worked with the multihyphenate, shooting his interior design projects, and has also turned his lens to the work of Pierre Yovanovitch, Kelly Wearstler, Rodolphe Parente, and Augusta Hoffman.

A kitchen by AKB Design in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec

Whether she is shooting portraits, food, travel, or interiors, Sylvie Li’s commercial and editorial images build a narrative. Just look at how she commemorates the marriage of old and new in this renovated Montreal apartment which appeared in AD.

The reception room of the barn on designer Jean-Louis Denoit’s watercress farm in France.

If Laura Gonzalez, Hugo Toro, and Pierre Yovanovitch feature on your list of design heroes, Stephan Julliard’s portfolio warrants a visit. The Paris photographer has worked with all three, as well as Jean-Louis Deniot, Kelly Wearstler, and Greg Natale.

Designer Meg Sharpe turns a traditional warren of rooms into an airy idyll where livability and flair are winsome bedfellows

Having shot for Dimorestudio, MacGuffin, Icon, and—hello, AD—Kyle Knodell has a knack for producing interior photos filled with life. At AD, we’ve tapped him to photograph Samantha Angelo and Peter Ostrega in their LES home.

The Paris apartment belonging to Gregoire Marot and Thomas Dupré de St Maur, designed with help of their friend the designer Eric Allart

Spain and Uruguay make appealing bookends for Ricardo Labougle’s practice. In between, his lens takes in interiors, gardens, and portraits, with the work of Jacques Grange, Vincent Van Duysen, Studio KO, and Michael S. Smith among its subjects.

A Stockholm apartment designed by Studio Escapist

From OMA’s architecture to Max Lamb’s furniture, Erik Lefvander moves easily between subjects, thrilling design enthusiasts. The Stockholm photographer’s collaborators also include Halleroed, Sabine Marcelis, and Sophie Dries.

Tour a London pied-à-terre by Studio Ashby that’s a dazzling foray into maximalism.

“Uplifting” is the best way to describe Kensington Leverne’s photography, thanks to the softness and warmth that her images exude. Whether the interiors she shoots are palatial or cozy, Leverne is able to evoke a sense of intimacy within each space.

A bedroom in Stockholm’s Ett Hem boutique hotel.

Magnus Mårding takes a natural approach, whether the subject is a person, a car, or an interior. Based in Stockholm, he has worked with Ilse Crawford, Michael S. Smith, and Olson Kundig. Different subjects, one curious eye.

Giulia Maretti can help set the scene as well as photograph it. The Bologna- and Berlin-based MAGI Studio cofounder combines photography, styling, and art direction, and has worked with the likes of MIDE Architetti and Studio Bosko.

A New York townhouse designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, Grace Fuller Marroquin, and Leonora Hamill

Mexico City provides a fitting home base for Fernando Marroquin’s design-minded lens. His subject matter ranges from interiors to hospitality to retail, and he has worked with Héctor Esrawe, Manuel Cervantes, Ezequiel Farca, and Luis Laplace.

Gabriel Chipperfield and Laura de Gunzburg transformed their 19th-century London flat, blending contemporary softness with crisp minimalism.

Multiple shoots for AD and Vogue that show the English country manors and London town houses of the UK’s top celebrities and creatives fill Kate Martin’s portfolio. She adapts her eye for fashion editorial to interiors and portraits with ease.

Nicolas Matheus’s photos have graced the covers of countless international design magazines, depicting chic French apartments, sunny Spanish casas, coastal Cape Town villas, and more. His work in and around the Mediterranean is particularly gorgeous.

Still-life arrangements of smaller objects within larger spaces populate Alice Mesguich’s Instagram feed, showcasing her penchant for capturing styled vignettes as well as corners and niches she finds interesting.

Fans of Ashley Montgomery, Sam Sacks, and Ali Budd may already have Lauren Miller’s images on their inspiration boards. The Toronto photographer captures interiors and still lifes, with work appearing in AD and House & Garden.

Balmore House in North London, designed by Studio 163

Architecture buffs will find familiar names in Peter Molloy’s orbit: O’Donnell + Tuomey, Grafton Architects, and Carmody Groarke, for starters. The London photographer has also worked with McLaren.Excell, keeping the built environment firmly in the frame.

In AD100 designer Vincenzo De Cotiis’s 15th-century Italian palazzo, a breccia baixa marble was chosen for its resemblance to the palazzo’s original ceiling, shown in this bath along with a circa 1895 Carlo Bugatti chair.

Textured surfaces—plasterwork, fabric, timber, you name it—are the first thing noticed in any interior shot by Martin Morrell, making him a favorite of designers like Vincenzo de Cotiis and Studio Peregalli. His full list of both editorial and advertising clients reads as a who’s who of brand and media.

A dining area in the famed Casa de Canoas, a Brazilian modernist landmark designed by Oscar Niemeyer. Parente shot a campaign for Zara Home here.

Fran Parente travels his São Paulo–New York circuit with some excellent design company. Studio Arthur Casas, Studio MK27, Studio Mellone, and Isay Weinfeld figure among his collaborators, while hospitality, travel, and food broaden his view beyond architecture.

The pool area at the Desert Rock Resort in Saudi Arabia.

BIG. Kengo Kuma. Heatherwick Studio. Ema Peter’s collaborator list could double as an architecture lover’s hot list. Working between Vancouver and Los Angeles, she doesn’t just specialize in architecture; she also photographs residential interiors, including projects involving Studio Paolo Ferrari.

Designer Jacques Garcia’s 17th-century apartment in Paris.

The bedroom of a New York townhouse designed by Greg Natale.

A private holiday home in Tuscany, Italy, designed by Vincenzo De Cotiis.

A room can tell a story, and documentary photographer Ambroise Tézenas has an ear for the details. Based in Paris, he has photographed interiors by Luis Laplace, Jacques Garcia, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, including commissions for AD France.

The kitchen in Nate Berkus and Jeremiah Brent’s home in Portugal.

Trevor Tondro’s command of color and mood brings a lively quality to his interiors photography. With early experience assisting both Philip-Lorca diCorcia and Martyn Thompson, he maximizes both artificial and natural light, always finding more than one way into a room.

Historic Castle Howard in North Yorkshire, London

If you find Simon Upton’s list of subjects resembles your decorating bookshelf, that’s understandable. Rose Uniacke, Rita Konig, Michael S. Smith, and Stephen Sills are among the talents whose work the UK-based photographer has captured across continents.

Devotees of Belgian design, take note. Antwerp-based Frederik Vercruysse has worked with Axel Vervoordt, Vincent Van Duysen, and Muller Van Severen—a particularly appealing trio for anyone whose saved images run from contemplative interiors to playful furniture.

This home in the Swiss Alps by activist Nachson Mimran and AD100 talent Francis Kéré graced the cover of AD’s January 2025 issue.

A farmhouse-inspired Manhattan apartment or a chalet in Megève? Cassie Floto Warner has photographed both for AD, including Amanda Seyfried’s New York apartment and a retreat by Elliott Barnes. The Paris-based photographer’s portfolio makes staying in sound particularly appealing.

Although he works all over the globe, Watson now lives in Dublin, where he was born.
